Let's dive into Chapter 6: Navigating Tricky Conversations—Staying Curious Under Pressure. As you get more comfortable with the coaching habit, you'll probably notice something interesting—sometimes, just when the stakes are highest or emotions are running strong, it's harder than ever to stick to your coaching approach. That's when those old instincts kick in. Maybe you want to jump in with advice, take control, or just sidestep the tough issue altogether. But here’s the thing: these are exactly the moments when coaching makes the biggest difference. So, what do you do when the pressure’s on? The real key is to stay rooted in curiosity, even if the conversation feels a little uncomfortable or unpredictable. That means holding back from offering solutions right away, and resisting the urge to guide things toward an easy answer. Instead, let the essential coaching questions be your anchor—they help keep the dialogue open, and focused on genuine learning. Picture this: a team member comes to you, clearly frustrated about a project setback. Your first instinct might be to defend the process, or jump in with some reassurance. But what if, instead, you simply ask, “What’s the real challenge here for you?” That one question invites them to dig deeper into their own experience. It helps ease the tension, and encourages them to take ownership, rather than just looking to you for answers. When you find yourself in these high-pressure moments, there are a few practical steps you can take:
First, pause before you respond. Just take a breath and notice any strong reactions or assumptions bubbling up. Next, acknowledge the emotions in the room. You might say, “I can see this is frustrating for you,”—and do it without judgment. Then, circle back to your core questions. Use your coaching framework to gently guide the conversation back to exploration and understanding. These simple habits help create psychological safety—making it possible to talk about tough topics without blame or defensiveness. And over time, your team learns that even the hardest conversations can actually be opportunities for growth and connection. Let’s bring it into the real world. Imagine you’re a manager, sitting down for a performance review with someone who’s been struggling. Instead of just focusing on what’s gone wrong, you could start with the Foundation Question: “What do you want?” That helps you understand their aspirations. Then, follow up with the Strategic Question: “If you’re saying yes to this, what are you saying no to?” Suddenly, what could have been a tense, one-sided conversation turns into a collaborative problem-solving session. So, when you stay curious under pressure, you’re modeling resilience and openness. You’re showing your team that challenges aren’t something to avoid or assign blame for—but something you can face together.
